vocabulary.definition: The value a producer hashes to pick a message's partition — the same key always lands on the same partition.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A well-chosen, high-cardinality key spreads load evenly; a low-cardinality key can concentrate most traffic on one partition no matter how many total partitions exist.
vocabulary.example: I'd check the partition key choice before assuming a bigger partition count fixes the imbalance.

vocabulary.definition: One partition, and its consumer, taking disproportionate load because the partition key values aren't evenly distributed.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It doesn't show up as an error — it shows up as one consumer falling behind while its siblings sit idle, which is harder to diagnose than an outright failure.
vocabulary.example: Keying by country created a hot partition, since most of our traffic comes from one country.

vocabulary.definition: The hard limit on how many consumers in one consumer group can do real work at once, set directly by the topic's partition count.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A topic with 8 partitions can never be usefully processed by more than 8 consumers, no matter how much extra hardware is added.
vocabulary.example: We hit the parallelism ceiling at 8 consumers, since that's exactly how many partitions the topic has.

vocabulary.definition: The real per-broker overhead of having too many partitions — more open file handles, slower leader elections and rebalances, and more replication traffic for the same total data.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's why 'just add more partitions to be safe' isn't actually free, and why a validated number beats an arbitrarily larger one.
vocabulary.example: I pushed back on doubling the partition count again given the real over-partitioning cost at our current broker count.

vocabulary.definition: The gap between the latest offset written to a partition and the offset a consumer group has actually committed.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the single most direct signal of whether the current partition count and consumer scaling are actually keeping up with real traffic.
vocabulary.example: Consumer lag is climbing on two partitions, which is what told me we're under-provisioned, not just a hunch.

vocabulary.definition: A partition where one or more replicas has fallen behind or is unreachable — an early-warning signal, not yet an outage.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's a separate health signal from throughput sizing, but it matters for the same reason: a cluster under more load than it can keep up with shows symptoms here too.
vocabulary.example: I checked for under-replicated partitions as part of confirming the cluster could actually absorb the new partition count.

vocabulary.definition: The real, measured number of messages a single consumer instance can process per second before lag starts climbing.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the second half of the sizing equation — peak throughput divided by throughput per consumer is what actually determines the real partition floor. This is a general capacity-planning metric; the course's monitoring lesson covers consumer lag as the symptom this metric explains.
vocabulary.example: Once I measured throughput per consumer at about 2,000 messages/sec, the rest of the sizing math became straightforward.

vocabulary.definition: Changing a topic's partition count after it's already in use, which changes which partition a given key hashes to for every message already in flight.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's not a free, instant change — it's part of why getting the count right up front, rather than treating it as freely adjustable later, actually matters. This course's partitioning lesson explains how a producer picks a partition from the key and count; the operational cost of changing that count after the fact goes a step beyond what it names directly.
vocabulary.example: Repartitioning later would quietly change which partition every in-flight key hashes to, which is part of why I want headroom built into the number now.

languageUpgrades.professional: Partition count sets a hard ceiling on parallel consumers, not a throughput dial — I'd rather compute the real floor from peak load divided by per-consumer throughput than just double it.

exercises.title: Validating what a green CI check actually guarantees about deployment safety
exercises.situation: After a pull request's tests pass and the required status check goes green, a stakeholder asks if that means it's now safe to merge and deploy straight to production.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Yeah, the tests passed and the check is green, so it should be safe to merge.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It conflates 'the tests we wrote passed' with the much broader claim 'this is safe to deploy,' without naming the real gaps in between — test coverage that might not catch every regression, the absence of any rollback plan, and a deploy job that runs fully against production in one shot with no staged or canary step. It leaves the stakeholder believing a narrower guarantee covers more ground than it actually does.
exercises.professionalResponse: A green required status check proves one specific thing: the tests we actually wrote passed against the code as it exists right now. That's real and valuable, but it's a narrower guarantee than 'safe to deploy,' and there are at least three gaps between the two. First, coverage: a passing not_null and relationships test suite says nothing about a business-logic bug that none of our tests happen to check for, so a green check can still ship a real regression if the test coverage has a hole. Second, there's no rollback plan built into this pipeline — our deploy job runs dbt build --target prod directly, and because a dbt deploy doesn't restart a server, 'rolling back' actually means re-running the build from the last known-good commit, not flipping a switch, which is slower than people usually assume when they hear 'we can just roll it back.' Third, there's no staged or canary step — the deploy job either runs fully against production or doesn't run at all, so if something the tests didn't catch does break, every downstream consumer of these models sees it at once, not a limited subset first. None of that means the check is worthless — it's a real, necessary gate — but I'd want to add a post-deploy smoke test that checks a few known-good values in the production tables right after the build finishes, and an explicit, documented rollback runbook, before I'd call this pipeline's green check equivalent to 'safe.'

scopeBreakdown.quickReference: A passing CI check is being read as a full safety guarantee, not a specific, narrower one.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: A green required status check is being treated as equivalent to 'safe to deploy to production,' which overstates what it actually proves.

scopeBreakdown.label: Clarify
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Confirm whether the real question is about test correctness or full deployment safety, which are related but not identical.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Clarify what 'safe to deploy' actually needs to mean here — code correctness only, or real production deployment safety including rollback and rollout.

scopeBreakdown.label: Observe
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Name precisely what a green check does and doesn't guarantee — coverage gaps, rollback, and staged rollout are the three real gaps.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Identifying exactly what the green check proves (the tests that exist, passed) and the three concrete things it says nothing about frames the real scope of the question.

scopeBreakdown.label: Plan & Perform
scopeBreakdown.quickReference: Add a post-deploy smoke test and a rollback runbook as the concrete next steps, not just a general caution.
scopeBreakdown.explanation: Proposing a specific post-deploy smoke test and a documented rollback runbook, while honestly naming the missing staged rollout, turns the caution into concrete, addable pieces.

scopeBreakdown.label: Evaluate

vocabulary.definition: A branch protection setting that blocks the merge button until a specific workflow check passes, not just a visual pass/fail indicator.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Without this setting, a red X is cosmetic — the merge button stays clickable regardless, so 'tests exist' doesn't by itself mean 'tests are enforced.'
vocabulary.example: The required status check is what actually blocks this merge, not just the fact that dbt test ran.

vocabulary.definition: Repository settings on a specific branch, like main, controlling what must be true, such as a passing check, before a merge into it is allowed.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the actual mechanism that turns 'we're supposed to run tests first' from a policy people can forget into something enforced automatically.
vocabulary.example: I'd add a branch protection rule on main requiring this check before anyone can click merge.

vocabulary.definition: The specific event — like pull_request or push — that a workflow's on: block fires on, and which a job's if: condition can check to run only in one of those cases.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's what lets a pull-request check and a production deploy live in the same workflow file while never running the wrong one in the wrong moment.
vocabulary.example: The deploy job's if: github.event_name == 'push' condition is what keeps it from ever running against an unmerged pull request.

vocabulary.definition: The job in a workflow that actually applies a change to production, gated to run only on a real merge to the main branch, not on every pull request.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Separating it from the pull-request job is what prevents an untested branch from ever touching production, and prevents production from going stale because nothing ever ran against it.
vocabulary.example: The deploy job only fires on a push to main, which is exactly what a real merge produces.

vocabulary.definition: The dbt flag selecting which named block of profiles.yml a run uses, letting the same project point at a disposable CI schema or the real production schema without changing the project itself.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's what makes 'the same tests, pointed at a different database' possible, instead of needing a separate project for CI versus production.
vocabulary.example: The deploy job runs dbt build --target prod, while the pull-request job stays pointed at --target ci.

vocabulary.definition: A documented, actually-usable procedure for undoing a bad deploy, as distinct from simply hoping the next deploy fixes it.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: For a dbt deploy specifically, there's no server to restart — undoing a bad change means re-running the build from the last known-good commit, which is slower than people often assume when they hear 'we can just roll it back.' This is a general deployment-safety practice; the CI/CD lessons here teach how the deploy job itself runs, not a formal rollback procedure on top of it.
vocabulary.example: I'd want a written rollback plan, not just an assumption that re-running the last good commit counts as one.

vocabulary.definition: Deploying a change to a limited subset of traffic or consumers first, before rolling it out to everyone, so a problem the tests missed affects a small group instead of everybody at once.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Without it, a single dbt build --target prod either succeeds for every downstream consumer at once or fails for every one of them at once — there's no middle option. This is a general deployment-safety practice beyond what this course's single-job deploy pattern implements.
vocabulary.example: This pipeline has no canary step today — a bad change reaches every downstream model at the same time.

vocabulary.definition: A quick, targeted check run immediately after a deploy completes, confirming a few known-good values are actually correct in the live system, as distinct from the pre-merge tests that ran before the deploy.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It catches the specific case where the deploy itself succeeded with no error, but something about the real production environment made the result wrong anyway. This goes beyond what the course's deploy-job lesson covers, which stops at the build succeeding.
vocabulary.example: I'd add a post-deploy smoke test that checks a couple of known production values right after the build finishes.

exercises.title: Validating that stale dashboard data is the intended trade-off, not a bug
exercises.situation: A stakeholder notices the dashboard sometimes shows numbers a few seconds behind the source system and asks whether that's a bug that needs to be fixed.
exercises.beginnerResponse: That shouldn't be happening, let me go look into why the data is wrong.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It assumes 'stale' and 'wrong' are the same claim, without first checking whether this specific component was deliberately designed to favor availability over strict consistency. It gives no plan to actually validate the behavior against a stated target, so it either escalates a non-issue or, worse, provides reassurance with nothing measured behind it.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before I treat this as a bug, I want to check what this specific component was actually designed to do during a brief hiccup, because 'stale' and 'broken' aren't the same claim. This dashboard reads from a cache and read replica that we deliberately built to favor availability over strict consistency — in CAP terms, it's AP-leaning on purpose: during a brief network blip or replication delay, it would rather answer with a few seconds of slightly old data than refuse to answer at all. That's a legitimate, common trade-off, not a design flaw, as long as it's actually staying inside the staleness window we promised. So the way to validate this isn't 'look into why the data is wrong' — it's to measure the actual replication lag against the budget we set for this component. If we committed to a staleness SLA of, say, 10 seconds, and I pull the real replication lag metrics and see a p99 of around 3 seconds with occasional spikes to 7 seconds during peak load, that's the system behaving exactly as designed, comfortably inside budget — not a bug. If I pulled those numbers and saw lag regularly exceeding 10 seconds, that would be a real problem worth escalating, but it would still be a different problem than 'the data is wrong' — it would be 'the system isn't meeting its own stated trade-off,' which is a precise, fixable claim instead of a vague one. I'd also distinguish this from message loss entirely: delivery guarantees here are at-least-once with idempotent processing, so what's delayed is freshness, not correctness — no event is actually missing or double-counted, it's just arriving to this read path a little later than the source system.

vocabulary.definition: The result that a distributed system spread across a real network can't fully guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance all at once during a network partition.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Since partition tolerance isn't optional for any real distributed system, CAP really reduces to a single practical choice: favor consistency or favor availability when a partition happens.
vocabulary.example: CAP theorem is the reason this cache can answer during a brief network hiccup, at the cost of occasionally being a few seconds stale.

lessonLink.label: Trade-off Analysis — CAP Theorem for Data Engineers

vocabulary.definition: A system that, during a partition, chooses to keep answering requests even if that risks returning slightly stale data, rather than refusing to answer at all.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the deliberate design choice behind exactly this symptom — a dashboard that's occasionally a few seconds behind is what an AP-leaning read path looks like when it's working correctly.
vocabulary.example: This dashboard's cache is AP-leaning on purpose, which is why it stays up and slightly stale instead of erroring out during a blip.

lessonLink.label: Trade-off Analysis — CAP Theorem for Data Engineers

vocabulary.definition: Choosing the consistency-versus-availability trade-off per operation or per component, rather than committing to one setting for an entire system.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It explains why one part of a platform, like a payment ledger, can be strict while another part, like a dashboard, is deliberately looser, without that being a contradiction.
vocabulary.example: We use tunable consistency here — the ledger writes are strict, the dashboard reads are intentionally looser.

lessonLink.label: Trade-off Analysis — CAP Theorem for Data Engineers

vocabulary.definition: A delivery guarantee that retries whenever there's doubt a message was received, which risks occasional duplicates but never silently loses a message.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the real, achievable guarantee underneath most streaming systems, as opposed to true exactly-once delivery, which isn't actually achievable across an unreliable network.
vocabulary.example: Delivery here is at-least-once — nothing is actually lost, which is a different claim than nothing being delayed.

vocabulary.definition: The practical result of pairing at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing, so duplicates may arrive but never change the outcome.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's why staleness and data loss or duplication are different problems entirely — this system can be a few seconds behind while still never losing or double-counting a single event.
vocabulary.example: Processing here is effectively exactly-once, which is a separate guarantee from how fresh the displayed number is.

vocabulary.definition: The measured delay between a write landing on the primary data store and that same write becoming visible on a replica or cache a reader actually queries.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the specific, measurable number that turns 'the dashboard seems stale' into an actual answer — within budget or not. This course's CAP lesson explains why a component favors availability over strict consistency; the specific metric used to measure the resulting staleness goes a step beyond what it names directly.
vocabulary.example: I pulled the real replication lag numbers before concluding anything — p99 came in well under our budget.

vocabulary.definition: A committed upper bound on how out-of-date a read is allowed to be, against which actual measured staleness can be checked.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Without a committed number, 'is this too stale' has no actual answer — a staleness SLA is what turns the question into something checkable. This is a general operational practice; the CAP lesson explains the underlying trade-off a staleness SLA formalizes.
vocabulary.example: Our staleness SLA for this dashboard is 10 seconds, and the measured lag is comfortably inside that.

vocabulary.definition: A guarantee that, given enough time without new writes, all replicas will converge to the same value — but at any single instant, different replicas may briefly disagree.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the general name for the behavior an AP-leaning system exhibits, and explains why 'stale right now' doesn't mean 'wrong forever.' This is a standard distributed-systems term; the CAP lesson covers the C-vs-A trade-off it results from directly.
vocabulary.example: This is a textbook case of eventual consistency — the replica is a few seconds behind, but it will catch up.

languageUpgrades.professional: Before I call it wrong, I want to check whether this component was actually built to favor availability over strict consistency — a few seconds of staleness can be exactly what it's designed to do.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Replaces an assumption of a bug with a check against the system's actual intended behavior.
